uni-civil-steel.title: Design of Steel Structures (IS 800:2007 limit state method)
uni-civil-steel.description: A full B.Tech-style subject: limit state philosophy, tension members, bolted and welded connections, columns and bases, beams and plate girders, with worked numericals and standard labs. Independent study companion; always check the current code text.

outcomes: State the key properties of E250 steel

lessons.title: Structural steel: properties and rolled sections

scenes.text: A contractor must choose between E250 and E350 steel for a warehouse portal frame.
The designer reads yield and ultimate strengths from the code before picking a grade.

steps.title: Mechanical properties
steps.body:
Mild structural steel (IS 2062 grade E250) has yield stress **fy = 250 MPa** and ultimate stress **fu = 410 MPa** for thickness up to 20 mm. E350 has fy = 350 MPa, fu = 490 MPa.

- Modulus of elasticity E = 2×10^5 MPa
- Shear modulus G = 0.769×10^5 MPa
- Poisson's ratio = 0.3
- Density = 7850 kg/m³ (78.5 kN/m³)
- Coefficient of thermal expansion = 12×10^-6 per °C

steps.title: Stress-strain behaviour
steps.body: Mild steel shows a linear elastic zone, a yield plateau, strain hardening and necking before fracture. The long plateau gives **ductility**: a member can deform visibly before failure, which is why design codes demand yielding to govern before rupture where possible.

steps.title: Rolled sections
steps.body: Common Indian hot-rolled shapes: **ISMB** (medium I-beam), **ISLB** (light), **ISHB** (heavy, column-type), **ISMC** (channel), **ISA** (angle, equal or unequal), **IST** (tee), hollow tubes (square, rectangular, circular) and plates/flats. Properties (A, Ixx, Iyy, Zx, Zp, rxx, ryy) come from steel tables; designation ISMB 300 means a medium beam of 300 mm overall depth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using fy = 250 for thickness above 20 mm without checking the code table (strength reduces for thicker plates).
- Confusing fy (yield) with fu (ultimate): rupture checks use fu.
- Mixing mm and cm in section property tables.

lessons.title: Limit state design: partial safety factors and load combinations

story.title: Why not just use a factor of two?

scenes.text: An old engineer says: just keep stresses below half of yield. A young engineer asks why dead and live loads are treated differently.
Limit state design assigns separate factors to loads and to material, reflecting how uncertain each one is.

steps.title: Limit states
steps.body:
- **Ultimate limit state (ULS)**: strength, stability, fatigue, fire, overturning.
- **Serviceability limit state (SLS)**: deflection, vibration, durability, local damage.

Design condition: design action (factored load) ≤ design resistance (nominal strength ÷ material factor).

steps.title: Partial safety factors (IS 800:2007)
steps.body:
Material factors γm: **γm0 = 1.10** (yielding, buckling), **γm1 = 1.25** (ultimate stress/rupture), bolts γmb = 1.25, shop welds γmw = 1.25, field welds γmw = 1.5.

Load factors γf for ULS: DL + LL → 1.5 each; DL + LL + WL/EL → 1.2 each; DL + WL (uplift, dead load favourable) → 1.5 DL + 1.5 WL with DL at 0.9 when it resists uplift. Serviceability uses γf = 1.0.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A beam carries dead load 20 kN/m and live load 15 kN/m.

ULS (DL+LL): wu = 1.5(20 + 15) = **52.5 kN/m**.

SLS: w = 20 + 15 = 35 kN/m.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A plate with Ag = 2000 mm² of E250 yields at Tdg = Ag fy / γm0 = 2000×250/1.10 = 454.5 kN, not 500 kN. The 1.10 reduction is the material factor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying factored loads for deflection checks (use service loads), or applying γm0 twice.

scenes.text: A thin flange buckles locally long before the beam reaches its plastic moment.
Classification by width-to-thickness ratio predicts this in advance.

steps.title: Four classes
steps.body:
IS 800 Table 2 groups sections by local buckling:
- **Class 1 Plastic**: can form plastic hinge with rotation capacity.
- **Class 2 Compact**: reaches plastic moment, limited rotation.
- **Class 3 Semi-compact**: reaches yield stress in extreme fibre only.
- **Class 4 Slender**: local buckling before yield.

Parameter ε = √(250/fy), so ε = 1 for E250.

steps.title: Limits for rolled I and channels
steps.body: Outstand of flange (b/T): plastic ≤ 9.4ε, compact ≤ 10.5ε, semi-compact ≤ 15.7ε. Web with neutral axis at mid-depth (d/tw): plastic ≤ 84ε, compact ≤ 105ε, semi-compact ≤ 126ε. The overall class is the **worse** of flange and web.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Rolled I-section, E250: flange outstand b = 70 mm, T = 10 mm → b/T = 7 ≤ 9.4: plastic. Web d = 300 mm, tw = 6 mm → d/tw = 50 ≤ 84: plastic. The section is **Class 1**.

With b = 120, T = 10 → b/T = 12 → between 10.5 and 15.7: semi-compact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using full flange width instead of the outstand (half width minus half web thickness region), and forgetting that E350 steel has ε = √(250/350) = 0.845 so limits tighten.

story.title: A roof in a cyclone belt

scenes.text: A coastal shed must resist uplift from wind.

steps.title: Types of loads (IS 875)
steps.body: Part 1 dead load, Part 2 imposed (live) load, Part 3 wind, Part 4 snow, and IS 1893 earthquake. Special: crane loads, temperature, fatigue, erection loads.

steps.title: Design wind pressure
steps.body: Design wind speed Vz = Vb k1 k2 k3 k4. Design wind pressure **pz = 0.6 Vz²** (N/m², Vz in m/s). Force on a surface = (Cpe − Cpi) × pz × area.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Vz = 39 m/s → pz = 0.6×39² = 0.6×1521 = **912.6 N/m²**. With (Cpe − Cpi) = 1.1 and tributary width 5 m, load per metre run = 1.1×912.6×5 = 5019 N/m ≈ 5.02 kN/m.

steps.title: Why wind matters in steel
steps.body: Steel roofs are light, so uplift can exceed dead load. Check member reversal: a rafter in compression under gravity may be in tension under uplift.

steps.title: The design loop
steps.body:
1. Fix geometry, supports, grade of steel.
2. Compute characteristic loads and factored load combinations.
3. Do analysis for bending moment, shear, axial force.
4. Select trial section.
5. Classify section.
6. Check ULS (strength, buckling, connections).
7. Check SLS (deflection).
8. Revise and detail.

steps.title: Quick numerical
steps.body: Simply supported, span 4 m, wu = 25 kN/m: Mu = wL²/8 = 25×16/8 = 50 kNm; Vu = wL/2 = 50 kN.

lessons.title: Modes of failure and design strength of plates

story.title: The hanger that snapped at the bolt

scenes.text: A tie plate fractured at its bolt holes though the gross section was nowhere near yield.
Net section rupture was the governing mode.

steps.title: Three modes
steps.body:
1. **Gross section yielding**: Tdg = Ag fy / γm0
2. **Net section rupture**: Tdn = 0.9 An fu / γm1
3. **Block shear** at the end connection.

Design strength = least of these.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Plate 200×12 mm, E250, two M20 holes (d0 = 22 mm) across the width.

Ag = 2400 mm². An = (200 − 2×22)×12 = 1872 mm².
Tdg = 2400×250/1.1 = 545.5 kN.
Tdn = 0.9×1872×410/1.25 = 552.6 kN.
Governing: **545.5 kN** (yielding).

steps.title: Why 0.9
steps.body: The 0.9 reflects the lower ductility of the net section, so rupture needs an extra margin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Deducting holes from gross area for yielding, or using fy in the rupture formula.

activity.prompt: Plate 150×10, E250, one M16 hole (d0 = 18 mm) across width. Compute Tdg (kN). Ag = 1500 mm²

quiz.q: Which usually governs for few small holes in E250?
quiz.why: Small net area loss means yielding governs.

scenes.text: A gusset plate has holes in two staggered rows to fit more bolts.
A fracture can zigzag between holes, so more than one path is checked.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: An = [b − n d0 + Σ (p²/(4g))] t, where p = pitch (stagger) and g = gauge between the two holes in the chain. Check every possible chain; the smallest An governs.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Plate 180×10, d0 = 22, stagger p = 50 mm, gauge g = 60 mm.

Straight chain, one hole: 180 − 22 = 158 mm.
Zig-zag, two holes with one diagonal: 180 − 44 + 50²/(4×60) = 180 − 44 + 10.42 = 146.42 mm.
An = 146.42×10 = **1464 mm²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding p²/4g for every hole instead of every diagonal leg, and not comparing all chains.

activity.prompt: Using the example (b=180, t=10, d0=22, p=50, g=60, two holes in chain) find An in mm².

quiz.why: The p²/4g term adds area back.

scenes.text: Roof-truss bottom chords are angles bolted by one leg.
Connection through one leg causes shear lag, so the outstand leg is only partly effective.

steps.title: Rupture of angle
steps.body: Tdn = 0.9 Anc fu/γm1 + β Ago fy/γm0, where Anc = net area of connected leg, Ago = gross area of outstand leg, and β = 1.4 − 0.076 (w/t)(fy/fu)(bs/Lc), limited to 0.7 ≤ β ≤ fu γm0/(fy γm1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating angle like a plate with all area effective, and skipping the β limits.

activity.prompt: Using the example, compute the first term 0.9·Anc·fu/γm1 in kN (Anc = 730 mm², fu = 410).

quiz.why: β falls as bs/Lc rises, so larger Lc raises it.

scenes.text: A gusset tore along a rectangular block around the last bolts.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
Tdb is the smaller of:
(a) Avg fy/(√3 γm0) + 0.9 Atn fu/γm1
(b) 0.9 Avn fu/(√3 γm1) + Atg fy/γm0
Avg, Avn = gross, net shear area; Atg, Atn = gross, net tension area.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using only one of the two expressions, or deducting the full bolt hole for end-bolt tension area instead of half.

activity.prompt: In the example, compute Tdb (kN) as the lesser of the two expressions.

quiz.why: Half-hole is deducted along tension plane at an end.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Bolted and welded connections
courses.summary: Bolt grades and detailing, shear/bearing capacity, HSFG bolts, fillet and butt welds, lap-joint design.
outcomes: Apply pitch, gauge and edge rules
Compute bolt shear and bearing strength

scenes.text: A site engineer finds three kinds of bolts in the store.
Spacing rules keep the plate from tearing between holes.

steps.title: Bolt kinds and grades
steps.body: **Black (unfinished) bolts** grade 4.6: fub = 400 MPa, fyb = 240. **High-strength** 8.8 (fub = 800, fyb = 640) and 10.9. **HSFG** bolts transfer load by friction. Grade 4.6 means fub = 4×100 = 400 MPa and fy/fu = 0.6.

steps.title: Hole size and spacing
steps.body:
Clearance hole d0 = d + 1.5 mm for d = 12–14, d + 2 mm for 16–22 and 24, d + 3 mm above 24 (M20 → 22 mm).
- Minimum pitch/gauge 2.5 d
- Maximum pitch (tension) 32 t or 300 mm
- Minimum edge/end distance 1.7 d0 (rolled, machine-flame cut edges), 1.5 d0 for sheared/hand-flame cut
- Maximum edge distance 12 t ε

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: M20 bolt: d0 = 22 mm. Min pitch = 2.5×20 = 50 mm. Min edge = 1.7×22 = 37.4 → 40 mm in practice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using nominal diameter instead of d0 for edge distance, or mixing bolt grade with steel grade.

lessons.title: Bearing-type bolts: shear, bearing and bolt value

scenes.text: A 150 kN tie must be bolted to a gusset.
Bolt value is the smaller of shear and bearing capacities.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
Shear: Vnsb = (fub/√3)(nn Anb + ns Asb)/γmb, where Anb = net tensile area (≈ 0.78 × shank area), γmb = 1.25.
Bearing: Vnpb = 2.5 kb d t fu/γmb, kb = min(e/3d0, p/3d0 − 0.25, fub/fu, 1.0).

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.body: Efficiency = strength of joint ÷ strength of solid plate; typically 60–80 % for lap joints.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using shank area when threads are in the shear plane, and forgetting to round the number of bolts up.

activity.prompt: Compute Vnsb for M20 grade 4.6 (Anb = 245 mm², single shear) in kN.

lessons.title: HSFG bolts and bolts in tension

scenes.text: A bridge splice must not slip under repeated loads.
HSFG bolts are tightened to a proof load so friction carries the shear.

steps.title: Slip resistance
steps.body: Vnsf = μf ne Kh Fo/γmf, with proof tension Fo = 0.7 fub Anb, γmf = 1.25 (ULS slip), μf = coefficient of friction (surface-dependent), ne = number of effective interfaces, Kh = 1.0 for clear holes.

steps.title: Tension bolts
steps.body: Tnb = 0.9 fub An/γmb (≤ fyb Asb γm1/(γm0 γmb) ). Prying action from flexible end plates adds tension and must be considered.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Painting faying surfaces (lowers μf), reusing HSFG bolts, or ignoring prying.

lessons.title: Welded connections: fillet and butt welds

scenes.text: A fabricator can weld in a controlled shop; on site wind and access hurt weld quality.
The code reflects this with different γmw.

steps.title: Fillet weld strength
steps.body: Throat thickness t = K s, K = 0.7 for 60–90° fusion face angle. Design strength per unit length = t fu/(√3 γmw) with fu the smaller of weld or parent metal. Minimum size depends on thicker part: ≤10 mm → 3 mm; 10–20 → 5; 20–32 → 6; 32–50 → 8. Effective length ≥ 4 s; maximum size ≈ thickness of thinner part minus 1.5 mm for square edges.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
6 mm fillet, shop, fu = 410: strength = 0.7×6×410/(1.732×1.25) = **795 N/mm**.
For 200 kN: effective length = 200000/795 = 251.5 mm; add 2s = 12 mm for end returns → 263.5 → provide **265 mm**.

Field weld (γmw = 1.5): 0.7×6×410/(1.732×1.5) = 663 N/mm — 17 % lower.

steps.title: Butt welds
steps.body: Full-penetration butt weld: throat = thickness of the thinner plate; design strength equals the parent plate in tension/compression. Partial-penetration welds use reduced throat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using leg length instead of throat, ignoring end returns, and giving the same length for field and shop welds.

2. Compute shear and bearing capacity, take smaller.
3. n = Tu / bolt value, round up.
4. Arrange bolts within pitch and edge limits.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Compression members and column bases
courses.summary: Euler buckling, IS 800 column curves, effective lengths, design of columns, lacing/battens and slab bases.
outcomes: Design lacing shear and a slab base

scenes.text: Press a plastic ruler end-to-end: it bows sideways long before it crushes.
Euler explained this with slenderness.

steps.title: Euler
steps.body: Pcr = π² E I / (KL)², so elastic buckling stress fcc = π² E/(KL/r)². Slenderness λ = KL/r. IS 800 limits compression members to KL/r ≤ 180.

steps.title: Effective length factors (IS 800 Table 11)
steps.body: Both ends hinged, no sway: 1.0 L. Both fixed: 0.65 L. One fixed, one hinged: 0.8 L. One fixed, one free: 2.0 L.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the larger radius of gyration instead of the smaller (buckling occurs about the weaker axis) and using the actual length instead of effective length.

activity.prompt: fcc (MPa) at KL/r = 100, E = 2×10^5 MPa

quiz.q: Doubling slenderness reduces fcc by factor

scenes.text: Tests show columns fail below the Euler curve due to residual stress and crookedness.
The Perry–Robertson-based curves a, b, c, d capture this.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: fcd = (fy/γm0) / (φ + √(φ² − λ²)) ≤ fy/γm0, with λ = √(fy/fcc), φ = 0.5[1 + α(λ − 0.2) + λ²]. Imperfection factor α: curve a 0.21, b 0.34, c 0.49, d 0.76 (chosen from Table 7 by section and thickness).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting that λ here is non-dimensional, picking the wrong curve, and using Ag instead of effective area Ae for slender sections.

scenes.text: A column supports 600 kN factored load.
She tries a section and checks Pd ≥ Pu.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Assume fcd (say 100–130 MPa for λ about 80–100).
2. Required Ae = Pu/fcd.
3. Choose section, find r_min, λ.
4. Read fcd from the curve; compute Pd.
5. Check Pd ≥ Pu, λ ≤ 180, and local buckling class.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Pu = 600 kN; assume fcd = 118.2 MPa → Ae ≥ 5076 mm². Trial section Ae = 6000 mm², λ = 100: Pd = 118.2×6000 = 709 kN ≥ 600. Utilisation = 600/709 = **0.85** — acceptable.

steps.title: Economy
steps.body: Aim for utilisation 0.85–0.95; brace weak axis to reduce λ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Checking only the strong axis, and ignoring connection eccentricity.

scenes.text: A heavy crane column is made of two channels connected by bars.
The bars must carry a transverse shear.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Lacing/battens are designed for a transverse shear of **2.5 % of axial load**. Lacing inclination 40°–70° to the axis; slenderness of lacing bars ≤ 145; effective slenderness of a laced column is taken 1.05× the maximum actual slenderness (1.1× for battened). Batten columns: slenderness of each main member between battens ≤ 50 and ≤ 0.7 of the whole column slenderness.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Pu = 800 kN → V = 0.025×800 = 20 kN. Two planes of single lacing at 45°: each plane takes 10 kN; bar force = 10/sin45° = **14.14 kN**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the full shear for each plane when two planes share it, and exceeding the lacing angle range.

courses.summary: Plastic modulus, bending and shear capacity, lateral-torsional buckling, deflection and plate-girder basics.

lessons.title: Beam behaviour: elastic and plastic modulus

scenes.text: A beam still carries more moment after the extreme fibre yields.
The plastic moment capacity is higher by the shape factor.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Elastic section modulus Ze = I/y; plastic modulus Zp = sum of first moments of areas about the equal-area axis; **shape factor** S = Zp/Ze (rectangle 1.5; I-sections about 1.12–1.18). Mp = fy Zp.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Rectangle b×d: Ze = bd²/6, Zp = bd²/4 → S = 1.5.

Required Zp for Mu = 135 kNm (E250): Zp = Mu γm0/fy = 135×10⁶×1.1/250 = 594,000 mm³ = **594 cm³**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using Z (elastic) with plastic design formulas, and forgetting that plastic capacity needs Class 1/2 sections.

lessons.title: Design bending strength and shear strength

scenes.text: A 6 m floor beam carries factored 30 kN/m.
Check moment, shear and their interaction.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
Laterally supported: Md = βb Zp fy/γm0 ≤ 1.2 Ze fy/γm0 (simply supported) or ≤ 1.5 Ze fy/γm0 (cantilever); βb = 1 for plastic/compact, Ze/Zp for semi-compact.
Shear: Vd = Av fy/(√3 γm0), Av = h tw for rolled I. If V > 0.6 Vd the moment capacity reduces (high-shear).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Skipping the 1.2 Ze cap, and applying Md to a Class 4 section.

steps.title: Euler theory
steps.body: **Pcr = π²EI/Le².** Effective length Le: pinned–pinned L; fixed–free 2L; fixed–fixed 0.5L; fixed–pinned 0.707L. **Slenderness ratio** λ = Le/r, r = √(I/A). Valid for long columns (λ above about 100 for mild steel). **Rankine:** 1/P_R = 1/P_crush + 1/P_E, P_R = σc A/(1 + a λ²). Use I about the weaker axis.

steps.title: Solved examples

**Example 1.** E = 200 GPa, I = 1.2×10⁷ mm⁴, L = 4 m pinned: Pcr = π²×200000×1.2×10⁷/4000² = 1.4804×10⁶ N = **1480 kN**.

**Example 2.** Same column fixed–free: Le = 8 m → Pcr = **370 kN** (¼).

**Example 3.** r = √(1.2×10⁷/2000) = 77.5 mm for A = 2000 mm²; λ = 4000/77.5 = 51.6 (short; Euler not valid).

steps.body:
- Using Euler on short columns (it exceeds the crushing load).
- Using I about the strong axis.
- Wrong effective length factor.

steps.title: Stopping sight distance
steps.body: SSD = lag distance + braking distance = 0.278 V t + V²/(254 (f ± 0.01 n)), V in km/h, t = reaction time (2.5 s as per IRC), f = longitudinal friction coefficient, n = gradient in % (+ uphill, − downhill).

steps.title: Other sight distances
steps.body: Intermediate sight distance (ISD) = 2 × SSD. Overtaking sight distance (OSD) = d1 + d2 + d3 (reaction run, actual overtaking, opposing vehicle clearance); IRC gives about 470 m for two-way roads at 80 km/h. Provide OSD wherever possible on two-lane roads.

steps.title: Gauges in India
steps.body: Broad gauge (BG) 1676 mm, metre gauge (MG) 1000 mm, narrow gauge 762 mm and 610 mm. BG is the standard network. Gauge is measured between inner faces of the rail heads.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Rails**: flat-footed, common weights 52 kg/m and 60 kg/m (UIC 60); long welded rails reduce joints.
- **Sleepers**: timber, steel, cast iron, concrete (prestressed concrete is standard). Sleeper density written as M + x for a rail of M metres, e.g. 13 m rail with M+7 gives 20 sleepers.
- **Ballast**: crushed stone, 250–350 mm deep; distributes load, drains, resists lateral movement.
- **Fastenings**: elastic clips, pads. **Formation**: prepared subgrade.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 13 m panel with density M+7: sleepers = 13 + 7 = **20**; spacing ≈ 13/20 = 0.65 m. A 1 km track: 1000/13 ≈ 77 panels → ≈ 1540 sleepers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Measuring gauge centre-to-centre of rail heads, and treating ballast as a structural slab (it is a free-draining stone layer).

steps.title: Equilibrium cant
steps.body: e = G V²/(127 R), with G = 1.750 m (centre-to-centre of rail heads, BG), V in km/h, R in m, e in m. Maximum cant on BG = 165 mm; maximum cant deficiency 75 mm. Safe speed on a transitioned curve: V = 0.27 √((Ca + Cd) R) (C in mm).

steps.title: Transition curve and gradient
steps.body: Transition lengths are based on rate of change of cant and cant deficiency. Gradients: ruling, pusher, momentum; grade compensation on curves for BG 0.04 % per degree of curve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using G = 1.676 m for the cant formula, and exceeding maximum cant without limiting speed.

steps.title: Turnout
steps.body: A turnout comprises **switches** (tongue rails and stock rails), **lead rails** and a **crossing** (nose, wing rails, check rails). Crossing number N = cot α (right-angle method), e.g. 1 in 12; α = tan⁻¹(1/12) = 4.76°. Higher N means gentler turnout and higher speed.

steps.title: Signalling basics
steps.body: Signals: stop, caution, proceed; colour-light signals with track circuits and axle counters detect train presence; **interlocking** makes conflicting movements impossible; block working keeps a section clear between stations; Kavach is an Indian automatic train protection system.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 1 in 12 crossing: α = tan⁻¹(0.0833) = **4.76°**; 1 in 8.5: α = 6.71°. The 1 in 12 allows a diverging speed of about 30 km/h (typical).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing crossing numbers (1 in 12 is flatter than 1 in 8.5), and treating signalling as only coloured lights.

steps.title: Site selection

steps.title: Orientation
steps.body: Orient the runway so that wind coverage is **at least 95 %** with crosswind component not exceeding 10.5 knots (20 km/h) for runways ≥ 1500 m, 13 knots (24 km/h) for 1200–1500 m, 6.5 knots (12 km/h) for shorter runways. steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Wind of 25 km/h at 30° to the runway: crosswind = 25 sin30° = **12.5 km/h**, headwind = 21.7 km/h. Limit 20 km/h for a long runway → acceptable. A wind of 50 km/h at 30° gives 25 km/h > 20 → counts as not covered.

steps.title: ICAO corrections (basic length at sea level, standard atmosphere, level runway)
steps.body:
1. Elevation: +7 % per 300 m above MSL.
2. Temperature: +1 % per 1 °C that the airport reference temperature Tr exceeds the standard atmosphere temperature at that elevation Ta = 15 − 0.0065 h. Tr = T_ave + (T_max − T_ave)/3 (T_ave mean of average daily temps, T_max monthly mean of maximum daily temps for the hottest month).
3. Gradient: +20 % per 1 % effective gradient.
The total correction for elevation and temperature should not exceed 35 %.

steps.title: Common mistakes

rounds.q: Explain limit state design and why we use partial safety factors.
rounds.model: Limit state design checks that the structure does not reach ultimate or serviceability limits. rounds.q: Why do we provide stirrups in a beam?
rounds.model: Stirrups resist diagonal tension from shear, confine the concrete core, hold main bars in position and improve ductility.

rounds.q: What is the difference between a one-way and two-way slab?

scenes.text: On a G+3 residential job, a junior engineer asks why the drawing shows only 3 bars at the bottom of a 6 m beam when the old working-stress notes used more.
The senior engineer explains that the beam is designed so that steel yields first and the beam warns by cracking and deflecting before it fails.

steps.title: Limit states and partial factors
steps.body: Design checks **limit states of collapse** (flexure, shear, torsion, compression) and **serviceability** (deflection, cracking). Loads are multiplied by a factor, typically **1.5 (DL+LL)**. Material strengths are divided by partial factors: **γc = 1.5** for concrete and **γs = 1.15** for steel, so design steel stress = fy/1.15 = **0.87 fy**.

steps.title: Assumptions and the stress block
steps.body:
- Plane sections remain plane.
- Maximum compressive strain in concrete at the extreme fibre in bending = **0.0035**.
- Tensile strength of concrete is ignored.
- Rectangular equivalent block: compressive force C = **0.36 fck b xu**, acting at **0.42 xu** from the top fibre.
- Steel design stress is 0.87 fy at yield.

steps.title: Balanced limit
steps.body: The neutral axis depth is limited so that steel strain is at least yield strain + 0.002. This gives **xu,max/d = 0.53 (Fe250), 0.48 (Fe415), 0.46 (Fe500)**. Beams are designed as **under-reinforced** (xu < xu,max) because failure is ductile. For Fe415, **Mu,lim = 0.138 fck b d²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using fy instead of 0.87 fy in the strength formulas.
- Forgetting that the moment from factored loads is Mu, not the service moment.
- Mixing N·mm and kN·m: divide N·mm by 10⁶ to get kN·m.

lessons.title: Shear in RC beams: tau_v and tau_c

scenes.text: During inspection of a 20-year-old warehouse, an engineer finds inclined cracks at about 45 degrees near the support of a beam.
There is almost no flexural cracking at mid-span. The cause is shear, not bending.

steps.title: Nominal shear stress
steps.body: τv = Vu / (b d). Concrete alone resists τc, which depends on the percentage of tension steel pt = 100 Ast/(b d) and grade (IS 456 Table 19). The maximum permitted τc,max is **2.8 (M20), 3.1 (M25), 3.5 (M30)** N/mm²; if τv exceeds it, the section size must be increased.

steps.title: Stirrups
steps.body: If τv > τc the stirrups carry Vus = Vu − τc b d. For vertical stirrups: **Vus = 0.87 fy Asv d / sv**. Even when τv < τc, minimum shear reinforcement is required: **Asv / (b sv) ≥ 0.4 / (0.87 fy)**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Beam 250 × 500, d = 450, support shear Vu = 90 kN: τv = 90,000 / (250 × 450) = **0.80 N/mm²**. For pt = 0.84% in M25, τc ≈ 0.59 N/mm². τv > τc so design stirrups for Vus = 90,000 − 0.6 × 112,500 ≈ 22.5 kN (using τc = 0.6).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Vu at the face of support instead of at distance d from the face (for the usual case).
- Forgetting minimum shear reinforcement and max spacing: lesser of **0.75 d or 300 mm**.

scenes.text: Free-flow speed 80 km/h, jam density 120 veh/km.
What is the road's capacity?

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: v = v_f (1 − k/k_j); q = k v. Capacity occurs at k = k_j/2 where **q_max = v_f k_j/4** and v = v_f/2.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: q_max = 80×120/4 = **2400 veh/h**, at k = 60 veh/km and 40 km/h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using k_j for capacity density.
- Confusing time-mean and space-mean speed.

scenes.text: Lost time L = 12 s and flow ratio sum Y = 0.7.
Find the optimum cycle.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: **C₀ = (1.5 L + 5)/(1 − Y)** s. Effective green total = C₀ − L, split in proportion to y_i.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Y ≥ 1 (over-saturated; no valid cycle).
- Forgetting lost time.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: g_i = (C₀ − L) y_i / Y. Add amber as clearance; check pedestrian crossing time and minimum greens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing greens equally.
- Ignoring pedestrians.
